scenes.title: wake-ups a night, and the schedule was perfect
scenes.voice: Six wake-ups a night. Twelve hours awake, twelve hours asleep. On paper, the schedule was perfect. So why was this little girl waking up again and again? Let's look at what was really going on, because the answer is probably not what you'd expect.

scenes.title: "She's overtired. Cut the nap."
scenes.sub: Advice her mom heard from three different people
scenes.voice: Hi, I'm Tetiana, a baby sleep consultant. I've worked with more than five thousand families over eight years. This mom of a thirteen-month-old heard the same advice from three different people. She's overtired. Cut the daytime nap. At four in the morning, sitting by the crib, she was ready to do exactly that.

scenes.title: What the sleep diary showed
scenes.voice: But first we opened her sleep diary. And the diary told a very different story.

scenes.title: 12 hours awake, 12 hours asleep
scenes.voice: Twelve hours awake. Twelve hours of sleep. Three proper daytime feeds, with no snacking in between. That is not an overtired child. If her mom had cut the nap, her daughter would have gone to bed short on sleep, and the nights would have become even worse.

scenes.title: How sleep cycles really work
scenes.voice: So where were the six wake-ups coming from? To answer that, we need to talk about sleep cycles.

scenes.title: Between cycles, the brain checks: is everything the same?
scenes.voice: Sleep isn't one long block. It comes in cycles. At the end of each cycle, the brain partly wakes up and checks whether everything is the same as when it fell asleep. Same place, same feeling, same conditions. If yes, it slides into the next cycle. If something is missing, it wakes up fully.

scenes.title: She fell asleep at the breast
scenes.body: At night she looked for it again
scenes.voice: This little girl fell asleep at the breast. So between cycles, her brain looked for the breast again. And when it wasn't there, she woke up. That's where the six wake-ups came from. Not from the schedule, and not from being overtired.

scenes.title: It's not hunger. It's a sleep association.
scenes.voice: This is what we call a sleep association. It's not a bad habit, and it's not something you did wrong. It's simply how the brain works. The child is looking for the same condition she fell asleep with.

scenes.title: What we changed, without tears
scenes.voice: So what did we actually change? Two things, step by step, with no crying it out and no weaning.

scenes.title: Feeding separate from sleep
scenes.body: Daytime feeds at set times, no snacking
scenes.voice: First, feeding. Daytime feeds at set times, with no snacks in between, and separate from sleep. So the breast stopped being the way to fall asleep, and became simply food.

scenes.title: Falling asleep in her own crib
scenes.body: Mom right there, step by step
scenes.voice: Second, falling asleep. She learned to fall asleep in her own crib, with her mom right there next to her. Gradually, at her pace. When she falls asleep without the breast, there's nothing to search for between cycles.

scenes.title: Check tonight
scenes.body: How did your child fall asleep?
scenes.voice: Here's what you can check tonight. How did your child fall asleep? At the breast, in your arms, or in motion? And do they wake at fairly regular intervals during the night? If so, don't rush to cut the daytime nap. Look at when and how they eat during the day, and whether feeding has become the way to fall asleep.

scenes.title: Want a plan for your child?
scenes.voice: Every child has their own sleep need, and it can be worked out from a few days of their diary. If you'd like me to look at your child's day and build a gentle plan, message me on WhatsApp. The link is in the description. Thanks for watching, and I hope tonight is a little calmer.
